title: A Practical Remote Team Operating Manual
content:
A remote team needs to know what happens when the person with the answer is asleep. An operating manual should settle that question with ownership, response expectations, decision records, and an escalation route. It does not need to describe every possible interaction. It needs to make routine work proceed without requiring everyone to remain online together.

Start with the work item rather than the chat channel

Give each meaningful piece of work a durable home. That could be an issue, a project card, or a document with an identifier. Record the outcome, owner, current state, next step, and blocking dependency. Chat can announce a change, but the work item's current state should not require reconstructing yesterday's conversation. Use links to join discussions to the durable record.

For a small team, keep status values simple: ready, active, waiting, and complete may be enough. Explain exactly what “waiting” means and who can remove the blocker. Define completion through an observable result, such as an accepted design or a verified customer workflow. A merged change is not automatically a completed outcome if the intended behavior has never been checked.

GitHub's milestone documentation describes grouping issues and pull requests with descriptions, dates, and progress information. That is one implementation option, not a requirement to buy a particular planning tool. The manual's responsibility is to define what the group means; software can display closed items without knowing whether the underlying goal was met.

Write a communication contract people can live with

Separate normal questions, time-sensitive blockers, and incidents. Give each class a destination and an expected response window during working hours. Do not set a universal response deadline that quietly requires people in every timezone to monitor messages overnight. State which situations justify an interruption and who is actually responsible for receiving it.

The GitLab communication handbook provides a primary example of asynchronous communication and written conclusions from offline conversations. Borrow the principle of preserving context, while adapting channel choices to your team. An asynchronous default is useful when messages contain enough information to act; a vague “can someone help?” merely postpones the missing conversation.

A good request includes the decision needed, deadline with timezone, relevant links, work already attempted, and proposed next step. If a discussion keeps circling because participants interpret the problem differently, schedule a short live conversation. Afterwards, record the conclusion and unresolved questions in the work item. The meeting should reduce ambiguity rather than create a private parallel history.

Make decisions visible without requiring unanimity

For recurring decisions, name one accountable decision-maker, the people who must be consulted, and the people who should be informed. Consultation is not the same as allowing every participant to block indefinitely. State when input closes and what evidence would justify revisiting the decision later. This protects both autonomy and the ability to correct a mistaken assumption.

Use a short decision record containing the problem, options considered, selected option, reason, owner, date, and review trigger. Put rejected options in plain language so a new teammate does not restart an old debate unaware of its constraints. Keep speculation separate from established limitations. “The provider contract forbids this” requires a source; “we prefer fewer vendors” is a team preference.

A hypothetical three-timezone release

Imagine a hypothetical team with designers in Lisbon, developers in Shanghai, and a reviewer in Toronto. They need to release a new export feature. The work item defines success as an authorized user downloading the expected fields, with a permission-denied case checked separately. The developer owns implementation; the reviewer owns acceptance; one release coordinator decides whether the evidence is sufficient to proceed.

At the end of the Shanghai workday, the developer adds a concise handoff: the preview address, test account instructions through an approved private channel, expected output, known limitation, and exact review question. The developer does not paste credentials into the public issue. Toronto reviews the artifact and records a defect against the work item rather than sending a message to someone who is asleep.

When a serious access-control concern appears, the documented incident route is used. Routine layout feedback waits for normal working hours. The example is hypothetical; it describes a coordination design rather than a claimed productivity improvement. The important distinction is that urgency comes from potential harm and blocked outcomes, not the volume of messages someone sends.

Keep the manual small enough to remain true

Assign an owner to each section and include a review trigger such as a new on-call arrangement, timezone expansion, or change of planning tool. Link to detailed runbooks instead of copying them. Duplicated instructions drift independently, especially when one version sits in a personal document. A manual that points to an obsolete escalation contact can be worse than an honest gap.

Run a handoff rehearsal with a task the receiving person has not seen before. Ask them to identify the owner, evidence, next step, and escalation route using only the written record. If they need private background to answer, improve the manual or work-item template. This is an editorial evaluation method, not a standardized measure of employee performance.

Operating-manual checklist

  • Define the durable home and minimum fields for work.
  • State working-hour response expectations and separate incident urgency.
  • Name decision owners and consultation deadlines.
  • Write conclusions from live discussions into the shared record.
  • Keep credentials and sensitive customer details in approved systems.
  • Rehearse a handoff without relying on the original author.
  • Review owners and escalation routes after organizational changes.
excerpt: Create a remote team operating manual with durable work records, realistic response windows, decision ownership, and a concrete three-timezone handoff example.
